title: What is your workflow for generating smooth, fluid 2D animations?
author: gholias
selftext:
Hey AI devs!

I'm trying to figure out the best workflow for generating consistent 2D animations.

I'm able to generate beautiful, well-made static images with Codex/OpenAI, but I'm not having much luck with consistent, good animations. I've tried a few approaches:

* **Frame by frame:** With a low number of frames, like 3 to 5, it doesn't look bad, but the animation feels laggy, like clay animation, which bothers me. With more frames, the coloring and shading usually vary between frames, and I end up spending a lot of credits fixing the problems.
* **Bone animation using Spine:** I spent some time installing a Spine skill and training the agent on the Spine docs and examples, but the final result isn't natural or organic. I'm doubling down by giving the model smoother, more fluid Spine examples to learn from, but I'm skeptical it will improve the quality.
* **3D animations:** I ran some tests where I created a 3D model using Meshy/Tripo AI and loaded an animation from Mixamo. It worked great for ready-made animations, but whenever I need a custom animation, the AI fails miserably.

Has anyone been able to generate good-quality animations? If so, could you share your workflow and tools?


PS: The animation in the post is just an example I found on Pinterest to show the quality and smoothness that I'm trying to get as close as possible.

comments.author: RandomCSThrowaway01
comments.body:
Of course 3D animations made by an LLM from scratch are going to fail. It can barely "see" and you are giving it one of the hardest possible tasks in the domain. 

I will give you a hint however - go look up motion capture. I am not talking spending few thousands on a suit. I am talking the software type that can run using your phone's camera. It's not perfect and the results are "dirty" but this is the kind of work LLM CAN actually do to clean it up and transfer over to your models.

Of course - this works for humanoids and animations that are anatomically possible. If you are trying to achieve the style of, say, Ori and the Will of the Wisps - you cannot yet. These cannot be done by fiddling with numbers in Blender, in practice a lot of how they work is breaking the character in half and completely destroying their geometry - just so it looks fine from one angle but everything else is an abomination. 

>**Bone animation using Spine:** I spent some time installing a Spine skill and training the agent on the Spine docs and examples, but the final result isn't natural or organic.

You are using Spine wrong. Animations done using it WILL never look natural or organic, even when a human does it. They can look smooth/passable but they cannot look like the reference you have posted. 

The best example of accomplishing something "natural" is Darkest Dungeon 1 where authors deliberately left some spacing between key frames and made sure not to interpolate too much. You need to leave a bit to players imagination. 

But, in practice, it's an XY problem. You don't use Spine for the stuff like animations you have linked above. It's not meant for heavy deformations, blurs and redraws. Use it when you are making a game about robots for instance. Now the fact it doesn't seem "natural" is actually a benefit. 

And in general LLMs are much happier animating robots anyway by the way. Since now they can do it via procedural animations and since you, a human, also don't have a direct point of reference then it will feel a lot better as you won't look for minor imperfections.

replies.author: gholias
replies.body: This makes a lot of sense! I'm rethinking my approach and I saw someone suggesting use Sedence to generate the animation and Im trying that right now.

comments.author: Exhales_Deeply
comments.body:
My tests - this was early last year, and I've got a broad skillset to exploit for this stuff so take that as a grain of salt - but I found video models to be super capable for a lot of things. 

I was generating initial frames in... i think it was GPT? peak 'piss filter' days! Maybe early nano banana, I'm not sure. Because i was going for a sort of 32/64 bit sprite vibe, somewhere between Donkey Kong Country and Odin Sphere, the toon style fed the video generators with all the info they needed, and outlines stood out cleanly when scaled down (with a touch of post wizardry)

Basically, i'd generate all of the stills needed and make sure they were consistent. then, prepping for video, i'd center them in a 16:9 frame, allowing a lot of space for actions - not concerned about sprite size at this point; just knowing they'd be shrunk. I experimented with a few options but good old greenscreen turned out best for the background.

Then with video, this was google veo i think? i'd prompt pretty casually: "a videogame character walks" "a videogame character falls to the ground" "a videogame character punches" - etc. Results were mixed but more often than not 1 in 8 would be rad, so I'd pull that.

Then i'd crop, key out the greenscreen, and retime to my heart's desire in after effects, before scaling down and crushing the color pallette.

I'd play with some hold frames just to demo them, but generally i'd program any holds into the game animation.

tl;dr: try a video generator

comments.author: mechatui
comments.body: I build models and animation myself and then get it to help rig the models and also do touch ups.
